Asia/Ho_Chi_Minh (ICT, UTC+7)
record.notes: State Dept Vietnam page, read 2026-10-12: Vietnam has ONE time zone and does NOT observe daylight saving, so the gap to the US shifts twice a year — 11 hours ahead of Washington DC during EST, 12 during EDT. Practical consequence for the audience: the arrival-day calendar date is almost always +1.

record.value: 220V / 50Hz. Sockets commonly take Type A (US flat two-pin), Type C (Euro round two-pin) and combined A/C outlets; Type F appears in newer hotels. A US two-prong plug usually fits physically — but 220V means a 110V-only appliance will be destroyed. Almost all phone/laptop chargers are 100–240V and need no converter, only (sometimes) nothing at all.
record.notes: The socket SHAPE is the part Americans get told about; the VOLTAGE is the part that costs them a hair dryer. Flag the dual-voltage check, not the adapter.

record.value: 220V / 50Hz; plug types A, C, and D (Type F also found in some buildings)

value: Any domain that is not evisa.gov.vn. The paid-intermediary market around the Vietnam e-visa is unusually aggressive: sites styled as official ('vietnamvisa', 'vietnam-evisa', '.org'/'.com' lookalikes) charge USD 50-100+ on top of the government fee for submitting the same free form. Some are legitimate agents; the issue is that the markup is rarely disclosed as a markup.
record.notes: Do not name specific domains in prose — they rotate, and naming one implies the unnamed ones are fine. The durable rule is the positive one: the government site is evisa.gov.vn and nothing else is.

value: Third-party sites charging extra 'service fees' for e-visa processing that are not the official government portal
Sites mimicking evisa.gov.vn with slight domain variations (e.g., evisa-vietnam.com, vietnam-evisa.org, etc.)
The defunct visa-on-arrival 'approval letter' system — any site still selling this for tourist entry is misleading
record.notes: The only official e-visa portals are https://evisa.gov.vn and https://thithucdientu.gov.vn. The Vietnam Immigration Department explicitly warns that the old immigration.gov.vn domain is no longer the operating portal. The U.S. Embassy directs applicants to evisa.gov.vn.

record.value: Six months beyond arrival.

Six months beyond the date of arrival, plus at least one blank page per entry stamp. Separately, and less widely known: an e-visa's validity must be at least 30 days SHORTER than the passport's remaining validity.
record.notes: The second half is from evisa.gov.vn's FAQ (https://evisa.gov.vn/faq), read 2026-10-12, verbatim: 'the validity of the electronic visa must be at least 30 days shorter than the passport validity.' This compounds with the 6-month rule and is the genuinely non-obvious part: a traveler whose passport expires in just over 6 months clears the entry rule but CANNOT be granted a 90-day e-visa — the system will cap or refuse it. No secondary source I checked states this. Strong candidate for a fact span. CONTRADICTION CONFIRMED 2026-10-12: travel.state.gov contradicts ITSELF on blank pages — its entry-requirements block says 'You must have 1 blank page available per stamp', while its E-visa warnings block says 'Your passport must have at least 2 blank pages required for stamps.' ChatGPT flagged exactly this internal conflict and was right; I had recorded only the 1-page figure. Write the conservative number (2+) and do not cite the page as if it spoke with one voice.

Vietnam abolished the 6-month validity requirement for Vietnamese citizens departing Vietnam (effective 15 August 2023), but the requirement for foreign nationals entering Vietnam may still apply in practice. The U.S. Embassy page opened does not state a specific passport validity rule. Confirm with the Vietnamese Embassy or airline before travel. Safe practice: ensure passport is valid for at least 6 months beyond intended stay.

record.value: Not stated as a legal entry requirement by the State Department. Airlines, however, enforce their own onward/return-ticket checks at US departure gates under carrier-liability rules — which is where an American actually encounters it.
record.notes: Distinguish the two: this is an airline rule, not a Vietnamese one. Articles routinely conflate them.

Airlines routinely require proof of onward travel or return ticket for Vietnam entry, especially for e-visa holders. Immigration officers may also ask. Not explicitly stated on the pages opened but standard practice across the region.

record.value: State Department guidance conflicts internally: one blank page per stamp versus two blank pages. It says e-visas cannot be extended domestically. Immigration separately describes possible sponsored new visas; that is not an e-visa extension. Sources: https://travel.state.gov/en/international-travel/travel-advisories/vietnam.html and https://evisa.xuatnhapcanh.gov.vn/trang-chu-ttdt. Special passport and exemption cases remain unresolved.

Entry rules attach to the actual passport, route and dates — not to 'American' as a label. A dual national entering on a Vietnamese passport, or a traveler arriving overland rather than by air, is under a different rule set.

Visitors are required to register their temporary residence with the local police station where they are staying overnight. Hotels typically handle this for registered guests; private stays (Airbnb, homestays) may require the host or guest to register. The U.S. Embassy notes this requirement applies to all visitors including Vietnamese. Airport authorities and airlines routinely check passports even for domestic flights. Children exiting Vietnam may require a Vietnamese passport or exit visa if they have Vietnamese parentage — contact the nearest Vietnamese immigration office.
Carry dong for street vendors and small purchases. Many hotels, restaurants and tour businesses accept international cards; acceptance is not universal.

Cash-first in practice. Cards work in hotels, chain supermarkets, malls and mid/upper restaurants in Hanoi, HCMC, Da Nang and Hoi An; street food, markets, most cafes, grab-a-bike fares, train and bus tickets bought locally, and nearly everything outside the big cities are cash. QR payment (VietQR) is near-universal among Vietnamese but normally requires a domestic bank account, so it is largely unavailable to a visiting American.
record.notes: The QR gap is the part Americans are unprepared for: they watch everyone pay by phone and assume Apple Pay will work.

record.value: Cash is king for street food, markets, small vendors, and taxis. Cards (Visa/Mastercard) widely accepted at hotels, mid-range and upscale restaurants, and many shops in major cities. QR code payments (VietQR) are increasingly common among locals. Carry small VND notes for daily transactions. US dollars are sometimes accepted in tourist areas but at poor rates; use VND.
ATMs accepting international cards are available at major airports and in cities. Arrange cash before visiting remote destinations.

Dense in cities and tourist towns, thin in rural north and mountain areas. Vietnamese bank ATMs commonly charge a withdrawal fee per transaction on top of the US bank's foreign-transaction fee, and many cap a single withdrawal at a low amount — which multiplies the fee against the total.
record.notes: The FEE and the WITHDRAWAL CAP are the useful numbers and I have not verified either; they vary by bank and change. Do NOT state amounts until a source exists. Flagged — the Thailand site shipped with an unresolved atm_fee span for months (see fleet memory).

record.value: ATMs widely available in cities and tourist areas (Vietcombank, Techcombank, BIDV, HSBC, etc.). Most dispense VND. Withdrawal limits vary (typically 2,000,000–5,000,000 VND per transaction). Foreign card fees may apply. Some ATMs in remote areas may be unreliable.
Declare cash exceeding USD 5,000 equivalent in foreign currency or VND 15,000,000 on entry or exit; these are declaration thresholds.
No limit on the amount brought in, but a written customs declaration is required above the thresholds: more than 15,000,000 VND, or more than 5,000 USD (or foreign-currency equivalent).
record.notes: State Dept Vietnam page, read 2026-10-12. Directly relevant to the customs/duty-free article. Note the asymmetry travellers miss: the obligation is to DECLARE, not to seek permission.

record.value: Travelers carrying more than USD 7,000 (or foreign currency equivalent) or more than VND 15,000,000 (approximately USD 950) in cash must declare to customs on entry or exit.
record.notes: This threshold is from a 2005 State Bank of Vietnam announcement reported by the Vietnamese Embassy in the US. Multiple recent secondary sources cite USD 5,000 or USD 7,000 as the declaration threshold — there is inconsistency. The official State Bank of Vietnam regulation should be confirmed before travel. Unlawful cross-border transport of foreign currency is punishable by fines up to VND 50 million per recent Vietnamese government sources.

record.value: No fixed national tipping rule. Restaurant and cafe tips are generally optional; tipping is more common for private guides and spa services.

Not customary and not expected in the way it is in the US; no tip is a normal, non-rude outcome. Tipping has become common in tourist-facing service (hotel porters, spa, private guides and drivers, Western-facing restaurants, cruise crews, where a pooled envelope at the end is the norm). Service charge appears on upper-end restaurant and hotel bills.
record.notes: The American failure mode is over-tipping from anxiety, not under-tipping. Frame the article around 'when it IS expected' — a short list — rather than a percentage.

record.value: Not obligatory in Vietnam. Tipping is appreciated but not expected in most local establishments. In tourist-oriented hotels, restaurants, and spas, small tips (USD 1–2 or 20,000–50,000 VND) are common. Tour guides and drivers may appreciate a slightly larger tip (USD 5–10 for a day tour). Taxi drivers typically do not expect tips; rounding up is sufficient. Bia hoi and street food vendors do not expect tips.

record.value: Vietnam Airlines
Vietnam Airlines (SkyTeam). Bamboo Airways, VietJet Air and Vietravel Airlines are the main other Vietnamese carriers; VietJet and Bamboo are low-cost and dominate domestic routes.
Vietnam Airlines (SkyTeam alliance); also Vietjet Air (low-cost), Bamboo Airways

record.notes: Schedules, fares, operating carriers and connection requirements from JFK, EWR, LAX, SFO, SEA, ORD, IAD and DFW remain unverified. No nonstop service is inferred.

PRICES are serve_live and must never be frozen. DURATIONS and ROUTING are stable enough to write: there is no nonstop from the US East Coast; Vietnam Airlines flies nonstop SFO-SGN and LAX-SGN (roughly 16-17 hours westbound), and everything else routes one stop through a North Asian or Gulf hub (ICN, NRT/HND, TPE, HKG, SIN, DOH, DXB). From JFK/EWR/IAD/ORD/DFW expect ~22-26 hours door-to-door with one stop. Total elapsed time, not flight time, is what the reader is actually planning around.

record.value: North–south passenger rail connects Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City via destinations including Hue, Da Nang and Nha Trang. Reunification Express describes services on this corridor rather than one unique train. Sleeper accommodation is available.

The Reunification Express runs the ~1,000-mile Hanoi-Ho Chi Minh City spine (roughly 32-36 hours end to end; almost nobody rides it end to end). It is used in segments — Hanoi-Hue/Da Nang overnight, and the Hue-Da Nang daytime leg over the Hai Van Pass, which is the one rail segment that is a sight in itself. Classes run from hard seat to 4-berth soft sleeper with air conditioning. Operated by Vietnam Railways; tickets are sold on the official site and at stations.
record.notes: The honest framing: the train is slower than the bus and far slower than flying, and is chosen for comfort and the Hai Van leg, not for speed.

record.value: Vietnam Railways operates the Reunification Express (Bắc–Nam) between Hanoi and Ho Chi Minh City, ~1,726 km, taking roughly 32–36 hours depending on service. Sleeper berths (soft sleeper with air-con, 4-berth; hard sleeper, 6-berth) and soft seats available. Book online via the official Vietnam Railways portal (dsvn.vn) or through authorized agents. Popular legs: Hanoi–Da Nang, Da Nang–Hue (scenic Hai Van Pass), Nha Trang–HCMC. Trains can sell out around Tet and holidays.
Intercity tourist buses include sleeper and reclining-seat vehicles. The tourism authority describes connections among Hanoi, Hue, Hoi An, Nha Trang, Da Lat, Mui Ne and Ho Chi Minh City.

Sleeper buses (reclining berths, not seats) cover every route, cost less than the train, and run overnight. They are the budget default and genuinely uncomfortable for a 6-foot American — the berths are built to a different frame. Open-tour bus passes (Hanoi-Hue-Hoi An-Nha Trang-HCMC) are sold by several operators.

Extensive long-distance bus network. Sleeper buses (giường nằm) common for overnight routes. Tourist-class open-tour buses (e.g., The Sinh Tourist, Hanh Cafe) cover the main north–south route with hop-on/hop-off flexibility. Local buses are cheaper but slower and less comfortable. Night buses can be cramped; motion sickness common on mountain roads.
Domestic air travel is available between major destinations. Date-specific routes, operating airlines, baggage allowances and airport terminals require airline verification.

Cheap, frequent, and the default for long hops: Hanoi-Da Nang or Hanoi-HCMC is roughly 1h15-2h versus 14-36h on the ground. VietJet and Bamboo undercut Vietnam Airlines heavily; VietJet's on-time record is the known tradeoff and its baggage allowance is sold separately.

Fast and relatively affordable for long distances. Major domestic carriers: Vietnam Airlines, Vietjet Air, Bamboo Airways, Pacific Airlines. Key routes: Hanoi–HCMC (2h 10m), Hanoi–Da Nang (1h 20m), HCMC–Da Nang (1h 25m), HCMC–Phu Quoc (1h), Hanoi–Phu Quoc (2h 10m). Book direct with airlines or via aggregators. Allow extra time at airports for check-in and security.
Grab operates in Vietnam; match the driver and vehicle to the booking.

Grab is the dominant app (car and motorbike taxi — GrabBike). Be (Vietnamese) and Xanh SM (electric, taxi and bike) are real competitors, Xanh SM increasingly so. Grab works on a foreign phone number and foreign card and is the single highest-leverage thing an American can install before arriving: it removes taxi meter disputes entirely by fixing the fare up front.

Grab (car and motorbike) dominates in major cities — Hanoi, HCMC, Da Nang, Hoi An, Hue, Nha Trang, Phu Quoc. Be (formerly Be Group) also operates. GrabCar and GrabBike are metered via app; cash and card payment options. Motorbike taxis (xe ôm) available but negotiate price or use GrabBike for transparency. Traditional taxis: Mai Linh, Vinasun (reliable in HCMC/Hanoi); avoid unmarked taxis.

record.notes: No complete, current legal determination was verified for an ordinary U.S. license, U.S.-issued IDP, Vietnamese license conversion, motorcycle category, engine or power exemptions, insurance coverage or alcohol limit. Rental availability must not be presented as permission to drive.

record.value: Drives on the RIGHT, and for a tourist the practical answer is: you cannot legally ride. travel.state.gov is blunt — 'U.S. driver's licenses and International Driving Permits do not work in Vietnam. If you drive without a Vietnamese license, you can be fined, arrested, or sent to jail.' Separately: 'Renting a moped or motorbike without a Vietnamese driver's license is illegal' and 'If you get in an accident without a license, your travel insurance may not pay your medical bills.' A Vietnamese licence is obtained through the Traffic Police Office of the Provincial Public Security and may require a medical exam. Self-drive car rental effectively does not exist for visitors; the normal product is a car with a driver.
record.notes: FULLY RESOLVED 2026-10-12 and it closes the project's former top blocker. DeepSeek's 1949-vs-1968 convention reasoning reached the right conclusion from the wrong (commercial) sources; the US government states it directly, which is both stronger and publishable. METHOD NOTE: this sentence is NOT in the page's rendered innerText — travel.state.gov hides large sections in collapsed accordions, so it only appears when you search the raw HTML. My first pass missed it and reported the question unresolved. Search the HTML, not the rendered text, on this site.

record.value: Driving is on the right side. US-issued International Driving Permits (IDPs) are NOT recognized in Vietnam because the US is a party to the 1949 Geneva Convention, while Vietnam recognizes only 1968 Vienna Convention IDPs. A US license alone is not valid for driving in Vietnam. Self-driving is strongly discouraged for short-term visitors due to traffic conditions, insurance complications, and the IDP issue. Most travelers hire a car with driver or use ride-sharing.
record.notes: Sources indicate Vietnam requires a 1968 Vienna Convention IDP. The US issues IDPs under the 1949 Convention. This is a significant practical barrier. Blood alcohol limit: Vietnam has a zero-tolerance policy for alcohol while driving (BAC 0.00). Fines for violations are steep. Verify current enforcement and any changes with the Vietnamese Embassy or a reputable car rental agency before considering self-drive.

record.value: Hanoi: cool or cold and misty December–March; hot, humid and rainy June–August. Hue: wetter September–February. Hoi An: wetter September–January. Ho Chi Minh City and Mekong Delta: rainy May–November, generally drier December–April. These are seasonal patterns, not forecasts.

Vietnam is ~1,000 miles north-to-south and has no single season — this is the defining planning fact. THREE regimes: (1) NORTH (Hanoi, Sapa, Ha Long, Ninh Binh) has four seasons including a genuinely cold, damp winter (Dec-Feb, 50s-60s F, grey drizzle 'mua phun'), a hot humid summer (Jun-Aug, 90s F, heaviest rain) and short pleasant shoulders (Oct-Nov, Mar-Apr). (2) CENTRE (Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An) is driest Feb-Aug and has a short, violent wet season Sep-Nov — typhoon season, and Hoi An floods most years. (3) SOUTH (HCMC, Mekong, Phu Quoc) is tropical and warm year-round, split into dry (Dec-Apr) and wet (May-Nov, afternoon downpours rather than all-day rain).
record.notes: The consequence no single-answer article can state: there is NO month that is good everywhere. Oct-Nov is excellent in the north and the worst of the year in the centre; Jun-Aug is good for the centre's beaches and brutal in Hanoi. This is a genuine swamp — an itinerary's shape is decided by it.

record.value: Vietnam spans multiple climate zones. North (Hanoi, Ha Long, Sapa): subtropical with four seasons — cool/dry winters (Dec–Feb, 50–65°F) and hot/humid summers (May–Sep, 80–95°F with heavy rain). Central (Hue, Da Nang, Hoi An): transitional — dry hot season Feb–Aug; typhoon/rainy season Sep–Dec. South (HCMC, Mekong Delta): tropical — hot year-round (75–95°F); distinct wet season May–Nov and dry season Dec–Apr. Central Highlands (Da Lat): cooler year-round, sweater weather at night. Phu Quoc: tropical; dry season Nov–Apr, wet season May–Oct.
Level 1 — Exercise normal precautions.
record.notes: Advisory issued 2026-06-24; checked 2026-10-12.

record.value: Level 1 — Exercise Normal Precautions. Date issued: June 24, 2026.
record.notes: travel.state.gov Vietnam page, read 2026-10-12. Level 1 is the LOWEST of four and the same level the State Department assigns to most of Western Europe — worth saying plainly, because the audience's prior is shaped by the war rather than by the current advisory. Change-prone: re-check before each publish and give it a short review_after.

record.value: Level 1 — Exercise normal precautions
record.notes: Date issued: June 24, 2026. This is the lowest advisory level. Advisory states Vietnam is generally a safe destination for travelers. Petty crime (bag snatching, pickpocketing) is common in tourist areas. Landmines/unexploded ordnance exist, greatest risk at construction sites, but risk is low in urban and tourist areas.

record.value: Petty theft; unexploded ordnance in affected areas.

Petty theft, overwhelmingly. State Dept, read 2026-10-12, verbatim: 'Vietnam is generally a safe destination for travelers. Petty crime is common, especially in popular tourist locations.' The dominant specific mode is drive-by phone and bag snatching from a moving motorbike, in Ho Chi Minh City above all. Violent crime against foreigners is rare. The genuinely under-weighted risk is ROAD TRAFFIC: motorbike injury is the leading cause of serious harm and medical evacuation for visitors, not crime.
record.notes: The risk an American fears (crime, residual war hostility) and the risk that actually hurts them (traffic) are different risks. The safety article should say so in the first paragraph.

record.value: Petty crime (bag snatching, phone theft, pickpocketing) in tourist areas; traffic accidents (motorbike-related); landmines/UXO in remote or construction areas; petty scams targeting tourists
record.notes: Traffic is the leading safety concern for visitors — crossing streets requires confidence and steady pace. Motorbike rental without proper license/experience is a major risk. Petty crime is opportunistic: keep phones secured, avoid dangling bags, be cautious in crowded markets and nightlife areas.

record.value: CDC recommends keeping routine vaccinations current, hepatitis A for eligible unvaccinated travelers and hepatitis B for unvaccinated travelers of all ages. Japanese encephalitis vaccination depends on duration, rural exposure and activities. Malaria prevention is itinerary-specific: CDC lists no transmission in Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City, Da Nang, Hai Phong, Nha Trang or Quy Nhon, but identifies rural risk areas. Arrange a travel-health assessment at least a month before departure when possible. These are health recommendations, not visa requirements.

Two different claims, and the article is the distinction. REQUIRED FOR ENTRY: none — the State Department says 'No vaccinations are required.' RECOMMENDED by CDC for Vietnam: Hepatitis A (unvaccinated travellers 1 year and older), Hepatitis B (unvaccinated travellers of all ages), Typhoid ('recommended for most travelers'), plus routine vaccines up to date and COVID-19. Conditional, not blanket: Japanese encephalitis (only for long stays or rural living), Rabies (dog exposure risk), Measles, Monkeypox (activity-based). Nothing is required at the border; all of it is a conversation with a travel clinic ideally a month out.
record.notes: CDC Vietnam destination page read 2026-10-12. The entry-requirement half is travel.state.gov. Keep the two authorities separate in prose — conflating 'required' with 'recommended' is the standard error in this article type.

record.value: CDC recommends: Routine vaccines (MMR, DTaP, varicella, polio, influenza) up to date. Hepatitis A (food/water), Typhoid (food/water), Hepatitis B (blood/body fluids), Rabies (animal contact, longer stays/remote areas), Japanese Encephalitis (rural areas, longer stays). Malaria: risk in some rural/forest areas; antimalarial medication may be recommended depending on itinerary. Dengue, Zika, and other mosquito-borne diseases have no vaccine — mosquito avoidance is key.
record.notes: CDC Vietnam page updated April 23, 2025 (page review date). Global Dengue notice (Level 1) issued September 3, 2026. Global Measles notice (Level 1) issued May 28, 2025. Consult a travel medicine provider 4–6 weeks before departure.

record.value: No — do not drink the tap water anywhere in Vietnam, including the major cities. Bottled and filtered water is universal and cheap; hotels and many cafes provide refills. Ice in established restaurants and cafes is commercially produced and generally fine, which surprises travellers who have been told to refuse all ice.

record.notes: Do not drink tap water. Bottled water widely available and cheap. Ice in tourist restaurants and hotels is generally made from purified water; street stall ice may be riskier. Brush teeth with bottled water if sensitive.

value: Taxi scams
Taxi meter manipulation and lookalike liveries — the reason Grab/Xanh SM is the standing advice: the fare is fixed before the ride and there is no meter to argue with.
The 500,000 / 20,000 dong note confusion at change — similar colours, a 25x difference. Learn the two notes before arriving.
Cyclo and xich lo rides where the agreed price turns out to be per person, per hour, or in USD.
Shoe-repair and fruit-basket approaches in Hanoi's Old Quarter: an unsolicited service performed before a price is named, then an aggressive price.
Motorbike rental damage claims — pre-existing scratches charged at return. Photograph the whole bike, with the renter present, before riding off.
'Closed today' redirection at major sights, steering to a commission shop or alternate tour.
record.notes: Every one of these is a price-ambiguity scam, not a theft. The single durable defence is the same each time: fix the price, in dong, before the service. That generalisation is worth more to the reader than the list.

value: Taxi scams: unmetered taxis or rigged meters; use Mai Linh, Vinasun, or Grab instead. Be wary of drivers who claim the meter is broken.
Motorbike rental scams: inflated damage claims when returning the bike; photograph the bike thoroughly before renting and document existing damage.
Street vendor overcharging: quoted prices for tourists can be 2–5x local rates; bargain or eat where prices are displayed.
Tour booking scams: fake travel agencies selling non-existent or substandard tours; book through reputable hotels or established operators.
Shoe shine / chewing gum scams: someone offers to clean your shoes then demands exorbitant payment; decline firmly.

Fake police: individuals claiming to be police demanding to see your passport or wallet; legitimate police do not typically stop tourists for random passport checks. Do not hand over your passport or cash.
SIM card scams: overpriced or non-functional SIM cards from street vendors; buy from official carrier stores (Viettel, Vinaphone, MobiFone).
Money exchange scams: shortchanging or offering poor rates; use banks, gold shops with clear rates, or hotel front desks.

record.value: Excellent and cheap. Viettel (widest rural coverage, state-owned), Vinaphone and Mobifone are the three carriers; Viettel is the default choice for anyone going to Sapa, Ha Giang or the Mekong. Physical tourist SIMs are sold at airport arrivals and require passport registration. eSIM is supported by all three and by the usual resellers (Airalo and similar), which is the lower-friction route for a recent iPhone — installed before departure, live on landing.
record.notes: Did not verify current data-package pricing and should not: it is serve_live. The durable facts are which carrier covers the mountains and that registration requires a passport.

record.value: Local SIM cards (physical and eSIM) widely available and affordable. Major carriers: Viettel (largest, best rural coverage), Vinaphone, MobiFone. Tourist SIMs with data packages available at airports, carrier stores, and authorized agents. eSIMs from international providers (Airalo, Holafly, Nomad, etc.) work and connect to Viettel/Vinaphone/MobiFone networks. Registration requires passport for physical SIM. Data is cheap — expect 10–30 GB for a few USD.

4G is near-universal including on most of the Ha Giang loop and in Sapa; 5G is live in Hanoi, HCMC and Da Nang. Dead zones are limited to deep karst valleys, parts of Ha Long Bay out on the water, and remote trekking. Wi-Fi is free and ubiquitous in cafes, hotels and many restaurants — more reliably so than in the US.

Excellent 4G coverage nationwide, including most rural areas. 5G rolling out in major cities (Hanoi, HCMC, Da Nang). Viettel has the widest rural and mountainous coverage. Remote areas (Ha Giang loop, deep Sapa valleys) may have spotty signal. Wi-Fi widely available in hotels, cafes, and restaurants.
record.notes: Coverage claims from independent network tests (2026) indicate Viettel dominates with 54–56% market share and best rural coverage. Secondary sources cite good overall coverage. Verify current coverage for specific remote itineraries.

record.value: Dress modestly at religious sites. Cover shoulders and knees; remove hats when entering temples or pagodas. Keep swimwear to beaches and resorts.

Day-to-day dress is relaxed and Western in cities; shorts and t-shirts are unremarkable. Two hard exceptions: temples and pagodas require shoulders and knees covered (and shoes off), and the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum in Hanoi enforces a strict dress code and bans shorts, bare shoulders, hats, cameras and phones inside. Beachwear stays at the beach.

Vietnam is generally casual. Lightweight, breathable clothing best for the heat. Modest dress expected at temples and pagodas: cover shoulders and knees; remove shoes before entering sacred spaces. Dress modestly in rural areas and when visiting homes. Swimwear only at beaches/pools. In cities, smart-casual is fine for most restaurants; very few places enforce dress codes. A light jacket or scarf useful for air-conditioned spaces.

value: Ask permission before photographing people.
Remove shoes before entering a private home.
Avoid public shouting or humiliating someone during a disagreement.
Offer or receive items with the right hand or both hands.
Xin chào means hello; cảm ơn means thank you.
Remove shoes entering a home, a temple, and many homestays and small shops — follow the pile of shoes at the door.
Hand and receive things — money, a business card, a gift — with both hands, or with the right hand supported at the elbow by the left. Small, noticed, easy.
Do not touch an adult's head, and do not point the soles of your feet at a person or an altar.

Public anger loses the argument. Raised voices cause loss of face on both sides and end negotiations rather than winning them; the smile that appears in a tense exchange is defusing embarrassment, not mocking you.
Photograph people only after asking, especially ethnic-minority women in Sapa and Ha Giang, where the camera has become an extractive transaction.

On the war: Vietnamese people are overwhelmingly warm to American visitors and the median citizen was born long after 1975. It is called the American War there. Museums present it from the Vietnamese side, bluntly — read that as a national account rather than a provocation.
Bargaining is expected in markets and with cyclos, not in shops with marked prices, restaurants or supermarkets. Do it lightly and stop once the price is reasonable.
DO remove your shoes before entering temples, pagodas, and private homes (look for shoe racks at entrances).
DO use both hands when giving or receiving items, especially to elders.
DO ask permission before photographing people, especially in rural areas and at religious sites. Some temples prohibit photography of certain statues.
DO dress modestly at religious sites — no tank tops, short shorts, or revealing clothing.
DO negotiate prices at markets, but do so with a smile — aggressive haggling is considered rude.
DO respect the elderly — offer your seat on transport, address elders politely.
DON'T touch anyone on the head or point your feet at people or religious objects.
DON'T be overly demonstrative with public affection — Vietnam is conservative about PDAs.
DON'T lose your temper in public — remaining calm and polite is highly valued and more effective.
DON'T discuss sensitive political topics (Vietnam War, government) unless your Vietnamese counterpart initiates.
DON'T hand items directly to monks if you are a woman — place them on a surface or hand to a male companion.
DON'T litter — Vietnam has a growing environmental awareness; dispose of trash properly.
DO learn a few Vietnamese phrases — locals appreciate the effort even if imperfect.
DO use a motorbike taxi (xe ôm) or GrabBike for short trips if comfortable — it's the local way.

record.value: Arrive through Noi Bai International Airport or by rail on the north–south corridor.

Noi Bai International (HAN), ~16 miles / 45-60 min north of the centre; longer in peak traffic. Grab, airport taxi and the 86 express bus all serve the Old Quarter. Rail and sleeper bus to Hue, Da Nang, Sapa and the south; short flights to everywhere.

Fly into Noi Bai International Airport (HAN), ~35 km (22 mi) from city center. Taxi (Mai Linh, Vinasun) or Grab ~45–60 min depending on traffic; airport shuttle bus (Vietjet, Vietnam Airlines) cheaper option. Train: Hanoi is the northern terminus of the Reunification Express. Overnight trains from Sapa, Lao Cai, and other northern destinations. Buses from Ha Long, Ninh Binh, Sapa.
Airport buses, taxis and ride-hailing are available.

Walkable in the Old Quarter and around Hoan Kiem — which is how most visitors should move, because the traffic makes everything else slower than it looks. Grab car and GrabBike for distance. Metro Line 2A (Cat Linh-Ha Dong) and Line 3 exist but serve commuter corridors, not the sights. Cyclos are a tourist ride, priced accordingly.

Grab (car and motorbike) most convenient. Traditional taxis (Mai Linh, Vinasun) reliable. Motorbike taxi (xe ôm) for short trips. Cyclo (pedicab) for sightseeing in Old Quarter — negotiate price first. Public buses cover the city but can be confusing for visitors. Walking is feasible in Old Quarter and around Hoan Kiem Lake. Scooter rental available but traffic is intense; ride only if experienced.
Noi Bai International Airport — HAN
Noi Bai (HAN) — international Terminal 2, domestic Terminal 1. Allow more time than the distance suggests.

Noi Bai International Airport (HAN). Two terminals: T1 domestic, T2 international. ~35 km from city center. Taxi ~VND 350,000–450,000 (USD 14–18); Grab similar or slightly less. Airport bus ~VND 40,000–50,000. Free Wi-Fi, SIM card counters, currency exchange, ATMs. Allow 2 hours for international check-in.
Accessible by air, train and bus.
Da Nang International (DAD) — the centre of the country's air network, with the most domestic routes and a growing list of international ones. Mid-point of the Reunification Express.
Taxis, buses and ride-hailing are available.
Grab; the city is spread along a beach strip and a river and is not walkable end to end. Hoi An is 40-50 minutes south, Hue 2.5 hours north.
Da Nang International Airport — DAD
Da Nang International (DAD), ~2 miles from the centre — unusually close
Tan Son Nhat International Airport serves the city.

Tan Son Nhat (SGN), unusually close — about 4 miles from District 1, but 30-50 minutes in traffic. Vietnam Airlines flies nonstop from SFO and LAX. Rail terminus of the Reunification Express; the hub for the Mekong Delta and Phu Quoc.
Taxis, ride-hailing and city buses are available.

Grab car and GrabBike dominate; a GrabBike through District 1 traffic is both the fastest option and the city's defining experience. Metro Line 1 (Ben Thanh-Suoi Tien) opened and is useful along its corridor but does not yet replace a Grab. The city is hotter, flatter and less walkable than Hanoi.
Tan Son Nhat International Airport — SGN
Tan Son Nhat (SGN) — T1 domestic, T2 international; the new T3 handles domestic traffic. Long Thanh, the future replacement, is NOT yet open.
No airport of its own: fly to Da Nang (DAD), then 40-50 minutes by car south. Hue is 3-4 hours north by road over the Hai Van Pass, or by train to Da Nang then car.

Nearest airport: Da Nang International Airport (DAD), ~30 km (19 mi) from Hoi An — ~45 min by taxi or Grab (~VND 350,000–450,000). Many hotels offer airport transfers. Train: Da Nang railway station, then taxi/Grab to Hoi An (~45 min). Reunification Express stops at Da Nang. Bus: local buses and tourist shuttles from Da Nang, Hue (~3–4 hours by road over Hai Van Pass).
Bicycle, on foot, and Grab for the beach. The Ancient Town is pedestrianised for much of the day. An Bang and Cua Dai beaches are 10-15 minutes by bike.

Walking is the best way to explore Hoi An Ancient Town (pedestrian-only at certain hours). Bicycle rental (~VND 40,000–80,000/day) for getting to An Bang Beach and surrounding rice paddies. Grab and taxis available for short trips. Motorbike taxi (xe ôm) for quick hops. Motorbike rental available but traffic in Da Nang (if riding there) is heavy.
Da Nang International (DAD)
Da Nang International Airport (DAD) is the primary gateway, ~30 km from Hoi An. ~45 min by car. Taxi/Grab ~VND 350,000–500,000 (USD 14–20). Many hotels arrange transfers. No airport in Hoi An itself.
Phu Bai airport (HUI) with domestic flights; on the Reunification Express; 2.5 hours from Da Nang by road or rail over the Hai Van Pass, which is the best rail hour in Vietnam.

Nearest airport: Phu Bai International Airport (HUI), ~15 km from city center; limited domestic flights (Hanoi, HCMC). Most travelers arrive via Da Nang (DAD) and travel by road/train (~3–4 hours) over Hai Van Pass. Reunification Express stops at Hue railway station. Tourist buses and private cars connect Hue to Hoi An, Da Nang, and DMZ sites.

The Citadel side and the hotel side face each other across the Perfume River and are walkable within themselves; Grab or a cyclo between. Royal tombs are spread out — a car, a motorbike or a river boat.

Grab and taxis available. Cyclo and motorbike taxi (xe ôm) for short trips. Walking feasible around the Citadel and Perfume River south bank. Bicycle rental for exploring the outskirts and royal tombs. Boat trips on the Perfume River to Thien Mu Pagoda and tombs.
Phu Bai International (HUI), domestic-focused
Phu Bai International Airport (HUI) — limited domestic flights from Hanoi and HCMC. Most international travelers use Da Nang (DAD) and transfer by road (~3 hours).
Phu Quoc International (PQC); ~1 hour from HCMC, ~2 from Hanoi. Fast ferries from Rach Gia and Ha Tien in the Mekong Delta.

Fly into Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC) — direct flights from Hanoi, HCMC, Da Nang, and some international routes (Seoul, Bangkok, Kuala Lumpur, etc.). Flight from HCMC ~1 hour; from Hanoi ~2h 10m. Ferry from Ha Tien or Rach Gia on the mainland (~2.5 hours). No train service.
Grab operates but thinly outside the main strip; most visitors use hotel transfers, taxis or a rented scooter. The island is larger than it looks — about 30 miles long.

Grab available on the island. Taxis (Mai Linh, local companies) available. Motorbike rental common (~VND 150,000–250,000/day) — island roads are quieter than mainland cities but still require caution. Bicycle rental for short distances. Many resorts offer shuttle services. Public buses (VinBus) on some routes.
Phu Quoc International (PQC) — and an approved e-visa air border gate
Phu Quoc International Airport (PQC). ~10 km from Duong Dong town center; ~30 min to northern resort areas. Taxi ~VND 150,000–250,000 depending on destination. Grab available.
